description: We are AstroNexa, a team participating in NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026. Our project, LunaQuest: Mission Survival, is an interactive educational game that teaches children aged 7–12 about lunar exploration and survival. Players manage oxygen, energy, food, and safety while making decisions to protect their Moon base. We welcome creative teammates interested in game development, UI/UX design, programming, and space science. Together, we aim to make learning about space fun and engaging!
summary:
LunaQuest is an educational game created by our team, AstroNexa_2, to help children aged 7–12 explore what life on the Moon might actually be like.
We wanted to make learning about space more exciting by giving children the chance to become junior astronauts and experience the challenges of running a lunar base. Throughout the game, players face different situations where they need to make decisions about oxygen, energy, radiation protection and how to use their limited resources wisely.
What makes LunaQuest special is that every choice matters. Players can see how their decisions affect their mission, learn from mistakes, and try different ways to solve problems.
Using scientific information and resources from NASA as a foundation, we aim to make the challenges of lunar exploration easier to understand through fun missions and interactive gameplay.
With LunaQuest, we hope to inspire children's curiosity about space while helping them develop problem-solving skills and understand how real astronauts make important decisions.
details:
What it does

Luna-Quest: The Living Moon Colony is a single-player educational game for children aged 7–12. The player is the mission commander of a Moon colony inspired by the lunar south pole. Children walk into every functional building (habitat, mission control, greenhouse, workshop), meet eight human crewmates with their own routines and stories, and solve problems by measuring, repairing, planning and deciding. There are no quizzes, no combat and no permanent game over. Mistakes are explained and can be fixed.

Main use

Luna-Quest answers NASA’s Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Its main use is to teach children how a Moon outpost really works by making trade-offs between power, air, water, food, radiation and communications.

How it works

Each activity follows one loop: explore, discover, understand, choose, act, see the result, reflect. The colony systems are linked. Dust on solar panels lowers power, low power dims the greenhouse lights, and the child must decide what to protect first. Crewmates speak, gesture and react, so children read less. A knowledge journal records each concept the child met. Hints adapt to how the child plays. An optional Lunar Day mode lasts 30 Earth days, about one Moon day.

How NASA data supports it

DONKI: space-weather events drive radiation alerts and shelter decisions.

LRO CRaTER: radiation measured in lunar orbit.

LRO LOLA and Moon Trek: terrain and slopes for rover routes and building sites.

NASA SVS illumination maps: sunlight and shadow for solar-power planning.

LRO Diviner: surface temperature.

JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth positions.

OSDR: plant studies for the greenhouse.

Each value keeps its source, unit and evidence type: direct Moon measurement, orbital data, spaceflight or Earth analogue, or future concept.

Benefits and goals

Children learn three lessons: the Moon has no breathable air, power depends on sunlight, and space radiation is a real hazard. They also practise teamwork, systems thinking and careful decision-making. We hope to make space engineering something children can experience through play.

Tools and technology

A shared C# simulation core (.NET Standard 2.1) holds all the rules (power, water, air, heat, dust, food, radiation, incidents) and runs without a game engine.

Unity 6.3 LTS is the target for the browser version.

Godot 4.7.2 .NET is a possible desktop version using the same core.

3D assets are made in Blender and the data is stored as JSON.

Delivered now vs future plans

Delivered: the full game design document, the technical architecture, the crew and player data for all characters, the research and evidence-labelling system, and this demo presentation.

MVP scope in progress: one connected Moon zone, four enterable buildings (habitat, mission control, greenhouse, workshop), six optional activities and the knowledge journal.

Future plans: Arabic and English play, a teacher and family guide, more buildings and crew stories, and player-built colony expansion.

Limitations

All in-game numbers are simplified game values, not NASA measurements.

A solar flare or proton flux is not a radiation dose, and the game does not convert one into the other.

Apollo-inspired stories say where the real event happened. Apollo 12 and 13 problems occurred in flight, not on the Moon.

Future technology such as a surface fission reactor is shown only as a research concept.

The game is educational and does not replace real engineering or medical guidance.
